questions.question: Wei writes 3.5 and 2.678 one under the other so the two decimal points sit in one straight vertical line, then fills the empty hundredths and thousandths places of 3.5 with zeros. What is 3.5 + 2.678?
questions.explain: Line up the decimal points and write 3.5 as 3.500, then add: 0.500 + 0.678 = 1.178, so the sum is 6.178. The usual trap is sliding 3.5 over to the right edge so the 5 lands in the thousandths place — the decimal point, not the last digit, decides the columns.

questions.question: A student writes 7.3 above 2.456 with the decimal points lined up in one column, and writes 7.3 as 7.300 so every place is filled. What is 7.3 − 2.456?
questions.explain: Line up the decimal points, write 7.3 as 7.300, then regroup: 7.300 − 2.456 = 4.844 (check by adding back: 4.844 + 2.456 = 7.300). The usual trap is taking the smaller digit from the larger one in each column instead of borrowing.

questions.question: Two decimals are written one above the other with their decimal points in a straight line: 0.68 on top and 0.475 underneath, with 0.68 written as 0.680 so the thousandths place is filled. What is the sum?
questions.explain: With the decimal points lined up, add from the right: 0 + 5 = 5 thousandths, 8 + 7 = 15 hundredths (write 5, carry 1 tenth), 6 + 4 + 1 = 11 tenths (write 1, carry 1 one) — the sum is 1.155. The usual trap is writing the ones digit of a column total and dropping the carry, which makes the answer 0.1 or 1 too small.

questions.question: A whole number and a decimal are written one above the other with the decimal points lined up: 6 on top (written as 6.000 so it has three decimal places) and 2.475 underneath. What is 6 − 2.475?
questions.explain: Write 6 as 6.000 so the decimal points line up, then regroup all the way across: 6.000 − 2.475 = 3.525 (check: 3.525 + 2.475 = 6.000). The usual trap is borrowing for the decimal places but forgetting to drop the 6 down to 5, which leaves the answer 1 too big.

questions.question: Maya's water bottle holds 0.75 L. On the bus ride to school she drinks 0.485 L. How much water is left in the bottle?
questions.explain: Line up the decimal points and write 0.75 as 0.750, then subtract with regrouping: 0.750 − 0.485 = 0.265 L (check: 0.265 + 0.485 = 0.750). The usual trap is subtracting the smaller digit from the larger one in each column instead of borrowing.

questions.question: Jayden rides his bike 1.2 km from home to the SkyTrain station, then 0.875 km from the station to his soccer field. How far does he ride in total?
questions.explain: Line up the decimal points and write 1.2 as 1.200, then add: 1.200 + 0.875 = 2.075 km. The usual trap is pushing 1.2 to the right so the 2 lands in the thousandths place — always match tenths with tenths and hundredths with hundredths.

questions.question: Which description tells you the correct way to set up and finish 9.4 + 0.836?
options: Slide 0.836 across so its last digit sits right under the 4 in 9.4, then add the columns.
Line up the decimal points, add each column, and whenever a column total is more than 9 just write the ones digit and move on.
Line up the decimal points, write 9.4 as 9.400 so every place is filled, then add from the right and carry whenever a column total reaches 10.
Rewrite 9.4 as 9.004 so it has three decimal places, then line up the decimal points and add.
questions.explain: Lining up the decimal points keeps tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths, and the zeros in 9.400 are placeholders that do not change the value, so 9.400 + 0.836 = 10.236. Two common traps are matching the right-hand edges instead of the decimal points, and dropping a carry when a column reaches 10.

questions.question: A bannock recipe needs 0.625 kg of flour. Ana has 0.47 kg in the jar. How much more flour does she need?
questions.explain: Line up the decimal points and write 0.47 as 0.470, then subtract with regrouping: 0.625 − 0.470 = 0.155 kg (check: 0.155 + 0.470 = 0.625). The usual trap is writing 0.47 as 0.047 or 0.407 — the zero placeholder goes on the end, never in front of the digits already there.

questions.question: Ravi's jug holds 1.5 L of juice for the class picnic. He pours 0.375 L into one bottle and 0.24 L into another bottle. How much juice is left in the jug?
questions.explain: First add what was poured out with the decimal points lined up: 0.375 + 0.240 = 0.615 L, then subtract from 1.500 to get 0.885 L. Two traps hide here — losing the carry when 7 + 4 makes 11 hundredths, and writing 0.24 as 0.024 by matching the right edges.

questions.question: Nora added 3.8 + 1.284 by writing the two numbers so their last digits lined up at the right edge, and she got 1.322. Her setup was wrong. What is the correct sum?
questions.explain: Nora's right-edge setup put the 3 and the 8 into the hundredths and thousandths places, so she really added only 0.038; lining up the decimal points and writing 3.8 as 3.800 gives 3.800 + 1.284 = 5.084. Estimating first also catches it: about 4 plus about 1 must be near 5, not near 1.

questions.question: For a science project, three students measure the sticks they collected at the park: 0.485 m, 0.5 m and 1.24 m. What is the total length of the three sticks?
questions.explain: Write them all with three decimal places and the decimal points lined up — 0.485 + 0.500 + 1.240 — then add from the right, carrying twice, to get 2.225 m. The usual traps are dropping one of those carries, which leaves the answer 0.1 or 1 too small, and writing 0.5 as 0.005 by matching the right edges.

questions.question: At the school track meet, Ella's long jump is 1.85 m and Tomas's long jump is 1.987 m. Their team needs the two jumps to add up to 4 m to earn the badge. How much more distance do they still need?
questions.explain: Add the jumps with the decimal points lined up: 1.850 + 1.987 = 3.837 m, then take that from 4.000 to get 0.163 m. Watch two traps — the carry out of the hundredths column in the addition, and dropping the 4 down to 3 when you regroup in 4.000 − 3.837.
